nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Tropical sun on the equator drives growth of mangroves, seagrass and forest trees along this coast.

nodes.name: Tides and salt water
nodes.desc: Tides flood and drain the mangrove mud twice a day, bringing salt water that mangroves tolerate and most other plants do not.

nodes.name: Monsoon rains
nodes.desc: Seasonal monsoon rains bring the freshwater that coastal forest plants and river-fed mangroves depend on.

nodes.name: Nutrient-rich mud
nodes.desc: Oxygen-poor mangrove mud holds the nutrients released by decomposing leaves and wood.

nodes.name: Fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down mangrove leaves, wood and dead animals in the mud, returning nutrients to the system.

nodes.name: Grey mangrove
nodes.desc: A salt-tolerant mangrove tree of Indian Ocean shores that holds muddy shorelines together and shelters young fish and crabs.

nodes.name: Red mangrove
nodes.desc: A stilt-rooted mangrove of tidal creeks in the Indian Ocean region. Its tangled roots shelter small animals and trap sediment.

nodes.name: Seagrass
nodes.desc: A seagrass of shallow East African and Indian Ocean waters, forming meadows that feed grazers and shelter small fish.

nodes.name: Grewia shrubs
nodes.desc: Shrubs of the dry coastal forest and thicket, recorded in GBIF data near the reserve. Browsers can eat their leaves.

nodes.name: Coastal forest trees
nodes.desc: Trees of the Somali coastal forest. A sapote relative, Manilkara sulcata, is recorded in GBIF data near the reserve.

nodes.name: Lesser kudu
nodes.desc: A shy browser of thornbush and dense cover. Tree and shrub foliage makes up most of its diet, and it is found across most of Somalia.

nodes.name: Dugong
nodes.desc: A large marine grazer that feeds mainly on seagrass. East African populations are now very small.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: Adults graze seagrass beds in shallow lagoons. Tiger sharks are the main predator of turtles of all sizes.

nodes.name: Mangrove crabs
nodes.desc: Small crabs of mangrove mud that feed on fallen mangrove leaves and so move mangrove nutrients into the mud and other animals.

nodes.name: Termites
nodes.desc: Termites eat leaf litter, roots and wood, including in mangrove forests, and are a major food for insect-eating birds.

nodes.name: Mud crab
nodes.desc: A large crab of estuaries and mangroves. Juveniles stay in the mangroves and the species is highly cannibalistic.

nodes.name: Sicklefin lemon shark
nodes.desc: An Indian Ocean shark that uses shallow sheltered waters such as mangrove creeks as a nursery.

nodes.name: Fork-tailed drongo
nodes.desc: A black insect-eating bird, recorded in GBIF data near the reserve. It hunts flying insects from perches.

nodes.name: Little bee-eater
nodes.desc: A small bird that catches flying insects on the wing; recorded in GBIF data near the reserve.

nodes.name: Von der Decken's hornbill
nodes.desc: A hornbill of dry bush and coastal woodland in East Africa. It eats insects and other small prey, and fruit.

nodes.name: Lion
nodes.desc: Top predator of the Lag Badana forests, which have been a Lion Conservation Unit since 2005. It hunts medium and large browsers.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: A large shark and the main predator of green turtles. Sharks also threaten young dugongs.
